problem: Prior VLN-CE agents (CMA, Waypoint Models, LAW, BridgingGap/CWP, Sim2Sim) are model-free and choose greedily among nearby predicted waypoints from a latent history state. This makes them shortsighted and opaque. VLN-CE success rates also trail discrete VLN by more than 20%.
motivation: Continuous environments with low-level actions demand strategic, long-horizon planning, and a pure RL signal may be too weak to implicitly learn an environment model. Cognitive-science world-model theory and model-based RL suggest a different route: an agent that can anticipate the consequences of candidate actions in an internal abstract world can plan better and explain its intent.
key_idea: Abstract the continuous environment into a discrete world model and run MCTS 'mental experiments' in it before executing low-level actions. The world model combines an episodic waypoint graph with a Pathdreamer-style scene synthesizer that imagines panoramic RGB-D views at unvisited waypoints, and a learned instruction-conditioned distance-to-goal function supplies rewards and the rollout policy.
insight: Most of the gain comes from look-ahead planning, not from the scorer. Greedy selection with the same distance function reaches 42 SR on val-unseen, below BridgingGap's 44, while MCTS planning over imagined futures reaches 49. Imagination quality matters: 'Copy Memory' (copying the nearest past observation) drops to 27 SR, and 'Perfect Imagination' (real future observations) gives 54, an upper bound of about +5 SR from a better world model. The dominant bottleneck is the learned distance/reward function. With GT distances SR reaches 100%, and replacing only 20% of estimates with GT already gives about 70 SR (figure only). Longer horizons help up to 4 steps, then degrade at 6 because synthesis error (FID) accumulates. Search iterations beyond 50 give only marginal gains while runtime grows linearly.
method: Waypoint action space: the CWP Waypoint_Predictor from BridgingGap outputs a 120-angle x 12-distance heatmap (3° bins, 0.25–3.00 m); NMS keeps up to 5 candidate waypoints, and the chosen one is reached with low-level actions.

Environment Graph (EG): an episodic graph whose nodes are visited waypoints embedded with panoramic RGB-D features and whose edges store (cos θ, sin θ, Δp). Edges exist only if two waypoints appear in each other's waypoint heatmaps; the start pose is (0,0).

Scene Synthesizer (SS): a two-stage Pathdreamer-style generator. It unprojects the current RGB-D plus RedNet-predicted semantics to a point cloud, reprojects it to the unvisited waypoint as sparse guidance images, then generates full panoramic RGB-D and semantics there. It is trained independently of the policy and chained for multi-step imagination.

Distance function F_d: a GAT over nodes [v, X] and edges [e_uv, u, X] (X from a bi-LSTM over GloVe), followed by an MLP (1,024 hidden units) that regresses each node's distance to goal. It is trained with L2 on EGs built along GT trajectories, each step adding up to 5 random accessible waypoints: 10 epochs on real observations, then 10 epochs with some observations randomly replaced by synthesized ones (AdamW, lr 2.5e-5, batch 16).

MCTS mental planning: tree nodes are (imagined) EG states and actions are any waypoint in the graph. Selection uses UCT with C=1.0, followed by expansion via SS, rollout, and back-up with γ=0.98. The plan uses 50 iterations and horizon 4; the root action with max Q is executed.

Reward and rollout: choosing an already-visited waypoint means stop and gives +5 if F_d≤3 m, else −5. Otherwise the reward is the change in D(s)=min_v F_d over graph nodes (paper writes D(s')−D(s)). The rollout policy samples from a softmax over F_d, with the discounted sum of up to K rewards as the leaf value.

setting.backbone: ImageNet ResNet (text says ResNet-18, supplement says ResNet-50) for RGB and PointGoal-pretrained ResNet-50 for depth (both frozen); bi-LSTM+GloVe instruction encoder; GAT+MLP distance function; Pathdreamer-style GAN scene synthesizer; CWP waypoint predictor — all trained on VLN-CE/MP3D
setting.training_data: R2R-CE (VLN-CE) train split: 10,819 instruction-trajectory pairs, 61 MP3D scenes. SS and the waypoint predictor are trained on MP3D train scenes following the Pathdreamer and BridgingGap schedules. No extra or augmented instruction data.
setting.observation: panoramic RGB-D (12 views at 30° separation; RGB 224x224, depth 256x256, 90° vertical FOV) plus instruction; RedNet-predicted semantics used inside SS
setting.action_space: predicted waypoints (≤5 candidates after NMS from a 120x12 heatmap) executed as low-level FORWARD 0.25 m / TURN 15° / STOP
setting.privileged: none for the main method; the 'Perfect Imagination' ablation uses real future observations, and the distance-function study replaces estimates with GT distances

numbers_note: The paper labels OSR as 'OR'. Table 1's caption is a copy-paste error (it is the SOTA comparison table). The text claims +7/+5/+7 SR over BridgingGap, but the table gives 59 vs 50 on val-seen (+9); Sim2Sim, not BridgingGap, is the strongest baseline on test SR (44). The distance-function study (100% SR with perfect distances, ~70 SR at 20% GT replacement) and SS FID-vs-step are shown only in figures. Other hyper-parameter rows exist: 70 iterations gives val-unseen SR 50 / SPL 44 at 1.74 s/step; horizon 6 gives val-unseen SR 48. The 'Copy Memory' ablation gives val-unseen SR 27 and is not listed above. The text is inconsistent on the RGB encoder (ResNet-18 in the main text vs ResNet-50 in the supplement).
results: On R2R-CE, Dreamwalker reaches SR 49 / SPL 44 on both val-unseen and test, and SR 59 on val-seen, beating all compared model-free agents. On test SR it beats Sim2Sim (44) and BridgingGap/CWP (42) with similar trajectory length. MCTS planning adds +7 SR on val-unseen over greedy selection with the same distance function (42→49). A perfect world model would add a further +5 (54), and 'copy memory' collapses to 27. Planning costs about 1.43 s/step with 50 iterations.
limitations: The learned distance-to-goal function is the main bottleneck (GT distances yield ~100% SR). The scene synthesizer is trained on only 61 MP3D scenes, so views are blurry for occluded or distant waypoints and for waypoints predicted inside walls, and synthesis error accumulates over horizons beyond 4 steps.
MCTS with generative rollouts is costly: ~1.43 s/step vs 0.09 s greedy, runtime grows linearly with iterations, and it may not scale to large environments.

Evaluated only in static Habitat simulation with no real-robot test. There are also internal inconsistencies: the reward sign D(s')−D(s), the rollout softmax over distance rather than negative distance, and the ResNet-18 vs ResNet-50 description.
